body:
What is defence indigenisation?

Defence indigenisation means developing the domestic capability to design, manufacture, maintain and improve equipment and technologies required for national defence. It aims to reduce excessive dependence on foreign suppliers, particularly for critical systems, components and technical knowledge.

Defence equipment includes aircraft, ships, vehicles, communication systems, surveillance equipment, protective clothing, medical supplies and electronic components. Therefore, indigenisation involves much more than manufacturing weapons. It also requires scientific research, skilled workers, reliable factories, testing facilities and suppliers of essential materials.

Defence self-reliance is the ability to meet important defence requirements with sufficient domestic technological and industrial capability. It does not necessarily mean that every component must be produced within the country.

Manufacturing in India is not always the same as indigenous development

A product may be assembled in India using imported parts, manufactured in India under a foreign licence, or designed and developed by Indian institutions. These situations represent different levels of domestic capability.

  • Assembly: Imported parts are joined to produce a finished product. Domestic assembly does not establish ownership of the original design.
  • Manufacturing: Production takes place in Indian factories. Some raw materials, components or technologies may still be imported.
  • Indigenous design and development: Indian institutions undertake the essential design and development work. This provides greater scope for modification, improvement and independent support.
  • Indigenous content: The specified domestic share of a product's value, calculated according to the applicable procurement rules. Under DAP 2020, the calculation generally deducts imported content, foreign services and fees paid abroad from the base contract price (total contract price less taxes and duties). It is not automatically the same as the percentage of parts counted individually.

For example, an aircraft assembled in India using a foreign design and imported critical components is not equivalent to an aircraft whose essential design and development were undertaken domestically. Both may support Indian manufacturing, but they involve different degrees of technological control.

Why is indigenisation strategically important?

A defence system must remain usable throughout its service life. Its parts may need replacement, its software may need updating, and its operators may require technical support. Dependence on foreign suppliers can create difficulties when imports are delayed, prices rise, technology access is restricted or international relations change.

Domestic capability can improve supply security, strengthen maintenance and repair arrangements, support skilled employment and allow equipment to be adapted to Indian requirements. It can also create opportunities for exports. However, domestic production must still meet standards of quality, reliability, safety and affordability.

What makes a technology dual-use?

Dual-use technology is technology that can have both civilian and military applications. Its classification depends on its capabilities and potential uses, not simply on whether it was first developed in a civilian or defence laboratory.

TechnologyCivilian applicationDefence application
Satellite navigationTransport, surveying and emergency responseNavigation and coordination
Unmanned aircraftCrop surveys and disaster assessmentReconnaissance and monitoring
Artificial intelligenceMedical-image analysis and industrial inspectionImage analysis and equipment maintenance
Advanced materialsTransport and protective equipmentLightweight structures and personal protection
BiotechnologyDiagnostics and vaccinesMedical preparedness and protective research

NavIC: an Indian example

NavIC stands for Navigation with Indian Constellation. It is India's independent regional satellite-navigation system, developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation. NavIC provides a Standard Positioning Service for civilian users and a Restricted Service for authorised users. It illustrates how an indigenous technological system can support civilian activities while also meeting strategic requirements.

The civilian and strategic services should not be confused with 2 completely separate satellite systems. They are services associated with the same Indian navigation programme.

Prelims focus

  • Indigenisation includes design, development, production, maintenance and technical capability.
  • Indian manufacture does not necessarily establish Indian ownership of the original design.
  • Dual-use technology can serve both civilian and defence purposes.
  • NavIC is an independent Indian regional satellite-navigation system developed by ISRO.
  • NavIC provides civilian Standard Positioning Service and authorised Restricted Service.
  • Trap: Dual-use does not mean that a technology must be used militarily.

[Sources: NCERT, Understanding Economic Development, Class 10, Chapter 2, Sectors of the Indian Economy; Defence Research and Development Organisation, About DRDO, Vision and Mission; ISRO, Navigation, sections on NavIC and its services; ISRO, Satellite Navigation Services, NavIC applications. Official websites consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Defence Indigenisation and Dual-Use Technology

body:
Defence capability depends on several institutions

Defence technology development is a cooperative activity. The Armed Forces identify operational requirements, researchers develop possible solutions, manufacturers produce equipment, and specialised agencies evaluate safety and quality. Government procurement connects these activities with the equipment required by the Services.

India follows a mixed defence-industrial model involving government research organisations, defence public sector undertakings, private companies, small enterprises, academic institutions and specialised testing establishments.

Defence Research and Development Organisation

The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) was formed in 1958. It operates under the Department of Defence Research and Development in the Ministry of Defence.

DRDO develops technologies and systems for defence and security requirements. Its work includes electronics, sensors, aircraft-related technologies, naval systems, materials, life sciences, computing and other scientific fields. It also supports testing, technology transfer and the transition from research to production.

DRDO primarily performs defence research and development. Manufacturing organisations produce equipment at industrial scale. A technology developed by DRDO may subsequently be manufactured by a public or private company.

Who performs the different functions?

Institution or participantPrincipal contributionExample
DRDOResearch, design, development and technical supportDefence electronics and materials research
Armed ForcesIdentify requirements, evaluate suitability and use equipmentArmy, Navy and Air Force
Defence public sector undertakingsManufacture, integrate and support defence productsHAL, BEL and BDL
Private industryDevelop and manufacture systems, components and servicesLarge manufacturers and specialist firms
MSMEs and startupsSpecialised components, software and innovative solutionsElectronics and sensing businesses
Universities and research institutesFundamental research, skilled people and applied innovationEngineering and scientific institutions

HAL means Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, BEL means Bharat Electronics Limited, and BDL means Bharat Dynamics Limited. These are public sector enterprises, whereas privately owned firms form a separate part of the industrial ecosystem.

Participation of private companies

India opened the defence industry to Indian private-sector participation in May 2001. This allowed domestic private enterprises to participate in defence manufacturing, subject to the applicable licensing and regulatory requirements.

Private participation may improve production capacity, increase competition and bring specialised expertise. Public-sector enterprises continue to play a substantial role. The distinction between public and private industry concerns ownership and organisation; it does not by itself determine the technological quality of the equipment produced.

Corporatisation of the Ordnance Factory Board

The production units of the former Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) were reorganised into 7 defence public sector undertakings covering 41 production units, effective 1 October 2021.

This was corporatisation: the former production units were placed under newly formed government-owned companies. It was not the sale of all those factories to private owners. The objective was to provide greater organisational autonomy, accountability and efficiency while retaining public ownership.

The new enterprises include Munitions India Limited and Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited, among others.

Why cooperation matters

A defence electronic system may depend on a researcher who develops the concept, a small company that produces a specialised component, a larger company that integrates the system and an independent establishment that checks performance. Even when the final product bears the name of one manufacturer, its development may depend on many organisations.

Prelims focus

  • DRDO was formed in 1958 and functions under the Ministry of Defence.
  • HAL, BEL and BDL are defence public sector undertakings.
  • Indian private-sector participation in defence industry was opened in May 2001.
  • OFB production units were reorganised into 7 DPSUs covering 41 units from 1 October 2021.
  • Public and private industry can both participate in domestic defence production.
  • Trap: OFB corporatisation in 2021 was not the same as privatisation.

[Sources: DRDO, About DRDO, Organisation, Vision and Mission; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, Setting up of New Defence Undertakings, 21 March 2022; Press Information Bureau, Splitting of OFB, 29 November 2021; Press Information Bureau, Ordnance Factory Board, 20 December 2021. Official websites consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: India's Defence Research, Public Industry and Private Industry

body:
Scientific development and equipment supply are different stages

A scientific idea does not become usable defence equipment immediately. It must be developed into a suitable product, evaluated against requirements, made reliable and produced consistently. A successful demonstration proves that an idea or system has achieved particular test objectives; it does not automatically mean that the Armed Forces have ordered or inducted it.

Major stages of technological development

  1. Identify the requirement: The intended user specifies the problem to be solved, such as a need for more reliable communication or improved protective equipment.
  2. Research and development: Scientists and engineers investigate possible solutions and develop an initial model or prototype.
  3. Evaluation and trials: The system is examined for relevant performance, safety, reliability and suitability requirements.
  4. Production readiness: A manufacturing organisation establishes the ability to produce equipment consistently and maintain quality.
  5. Procurement and supply: The authorised buyer completes the applicable acquisition process and places a contract.
  6. Service and improvement: Equipment is maintained, repaired and updated throughout its useful life.

These are broad stages, not a compulsory single sequence for every project. Testing and improvement may be repeated, and acquisition procedures vary according to the type of equipment.

Distinguishing testing, certification and procurement

TermMeaningWhat it does not establish
Prototype demonstrationShows that a proposed solution can perform specified functionsRoutine production
Testing or trialsEvaluates performance under specified conditionsGuaranteed acceptance
Quality assuranceChecks that required quality standards are met consistentlyOwnership of the design
CertificationConfirms compliance with a defined approval standardAn automatic purchase order
Procurement contractCreates an agreed obligation to supply equipment or servicesCompleted delivery or operational induction

An important Indian institution is CEMILAC, the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification, associated with DRDO. It provides airworthiness certification for military aircraft and other airborne platforms, including unmanned aerial vehicles. Its guidance specifically distinguishes type approval from an assurance of a production order.

Technology transfer

Transfer of Technology (ToT) is an arrangement through which an organisation provides another organisation with specified technical knowledge, documentation, assistance or rights needed to manufacture or use a technology under agreed conditions.

ToT can help industry produce a technology that originated in a research laboratory. However, the receiving company does not automatically acquire unrestricted ownership of patents, complete design rights or permission to export the resulting product. Those rights depend on the agreement and applicable law.

DRDO's Policy for Transfer of Technology 2025 distinguishes security-sensitive defence technologies from suitable dual-use technologies with commercial applications. Under the policy, certain dual-use or spin-off technologies may be licensed for appropriate commercial markets, subject to the specified conditions.

Indian programmes supporting innovation

Innovations for Defence Excellence

iDEX, or Innovations for Defence Excellence, was launched on 12 April 2018. It operates through the Defence Innovation Organisation framework and encourages startups, MSMEs, researchers and innovators to address defence and aerospace technology requirements.

ADITI

ADITI stands for Acing Development of Innovative Technologies with iDEX. Launched on 4 March 2024, it supports the development of critical and strategic defence technologies. At launch, the scheme provided for grants of up to ₹25 crore for eligible startups. ADITI is part of the iDEX framework, not an unrelated civilian science mission.

Technology Development Fund

The Technology Development Fund (TDF) is a Ministry of Defence initiative implemented through DRDO. It supports Indian industry, particularly MSMEs and startups, in developing defence and dual-use technologies that require domestic technological capability.

Access to government testing facilities

Testing equipment can be expensive, particularly for smaller enterprises. Access to government testing infrastructure helps domestic developers evaluate their products without independently establishing every specialised facility.

On 7 October 2026, the Ministry of Defence announced a revised procedure for industry access to proof ranges, field ranges and testing facilities. It waived proof and testing charges for specified Ministry of Defence developmental projects, including iDEX, TDF and Make projects. Charges can still apply in other cases. The waiver must not be understood as free testing for every private product.

Prelims focus

  • iDEX was launched on 12 April 2018.
  • ADITI was launched on 4 March 2024 under the iDEX framework.
  • ADITI provided for eligible startup grants of up to ₹25 crore at launch.
  • TDF is a defence and dual-use technology-development initiative implemented through DRDO.
  • CEMILAC is associated with military airworthiness certification.
  • Trap: A successful test, certification or type approval is not equivalent to a procurement contract.

[Sources: DRDO, About DRDO, Mission; DRDO, Certification Services, CEMILAC; DRDO, Policy for Transfer of Technology 2025, sections on technology categories and licensing, published online 13 January 2026; Press Information Bureau, Contract Signing of Army iDEX Project, 30 September 2024; Press Information Bureau, DefConnect 2024: Launch of ADITI Scheme, 4 March 2024; Press Information Bureau, Revised Standard Operating Procedure for Utilisation of MoD Proof Ranges, Field Firing Ranges and Test Facilities, 7 October 2026. Official websites consulted 14 November 2026.]
